content.symptom: the entire project plays back sped up or slowed down and pitched up or down accordingly (like a record at the wrong RPM) — not just one region, and not fixed by changing tempo or Smart Tempo settings
content.cause: the project's sample rate doesn't match the audio interface's actual output sample rate — Logic's engine and the interface disagree on how many samples per second make up a second of audio, so playback runs at the wrong rate
content.fix: Step 1: Open File > Project Settings > Audio and check the project's Sample Rate. Step 2: Open macOS Audio MIDI Setup (Spotlight search) and confirm the interface's own sample rate matches — some interfaces have a hardware switch or their own control panel that can override what Logic requests. Step 3: Set both to the same value (44.1 kHz and 48 kHz are the most common) and restart playback.
content.do_not: do not chase this as a tempo or Smart Tempo problem — tempo changes preserve pitch (time-stretching), a true sample-rate mismatch does not; if speed and pitch are both off together, it's the sample rate, not the tempo

content.symptom: a sample or recorded audio region sounds warped, sped up, or slowed down after being imported or after changing the project tempo
content.cause: Logic's Smart Tempo is set to 'Keep' or 'Automatic' and is stretching the audio to match the project tempo
content.fix: To fix one region: select it, open the Region Inspector (press I), click the 'Region:' disclosure header to expand it if needed, and set the 'Smart Tempo' dropdown to Off. To prevent it for all future imports: File > Project Settings > Smart Tempo > set 'Set Imported Files To' to Flex Off.
content.do_not: do not change the project tempo to try to match the audio — this affects the whole project

content.zone: low-mid resonance, roughly 100–300 Hz
content.remove_when: bass sounds unclear, conflicts with the kick, or makes the low end feel soupy
content.remove_move: narrow bell cut in the 150–300 Hz range; sweep to find the buildup peak on this bass
content.do_not: do not boost the sub (60–80 Hz) to compensate — that makes the problem worse on small speakers

content.zone: low-mid buildup, roughly 200–400 Hz
content.remove_when: vocals sound unclear, masked, or hard to hear in the mix
content.remove_move: narrow bell cut 2–4 dB somewhere in the 200–350 Hz range — sweep slowly to find where the buildup lives on this specific vocal
content.do_not: do not boost high frequencies to try to cut through the mud; remove the mud first, then judge

content.zone: low end, 60–200 Hz — kick sub weight and bass fundamental overlap
content.remove_when: the kick and bass sound like one unclear blob, cancel each other out, or the low end feels congested
content.remove_move: sidechain compress the bass to the kick, and EQ the kick and bass to own different sub zones — e.g. kick peaks at 60 Hz, bass peaks at 80–100 Hz
content.do_not: do not boost both the kick and bass at the same sub frequency — choose one to own that zone

content.zone: sub, 60–80 Hz; low-mid mud at 200–350 Hz
content.remove_when: bass is overpowering, flabby, or makes small speakers distort
content.add_when: bass feels thin, weak, or lacks sub weight
content.add_move: gentle bell boost at 60–80 Hz; cut 200–350 Hz to clear the mud that competes with the sub
content.do_not: do not boost sub without cutting the muddy low-mid zone — you'll add weight and mud at the same time

content.zone: stereo field; mid/side balance
content.add_when: mix sounds narrow, mono-ish, or elements feel crowded in the center
content.add_move: pan complementary elements away from center; use Stereo Spread on pads/synths/reverb; keep bass and kick mono below 100–150 Hz
content.remove_when: mix doesn't translate to mono, sounds hollow in the center, or elements phase-cancel
content.do_not: do not widen the bass below 100–150 Hz — it causes phase cancellation in mono

content.zone: stereo field — phase relationship between L and R channels, especially below 200 Hz
content.remove_when: the mix sounds full and wide in stereo but becomes thin, hollow, or loses instruments when played in mono (phone speaker, Bluetooth)
content.remove_move: mono the mix and solo tracks one by one to find what disappears; common culprits are stereo widening on bass, out-of-phase samples, or a doubled vocal that phase-cancels
content.do_not: do not assume a mix that sounds wide in stereo will translate to mono — always check in mono before finishing

content.symptom: meters move but no audio from speakers or headphones
content.cause: output routing mismatch, muted master, or wrong audio device selected
content.fix: check the master fader is not muted; open Logic Pro > Settings > Audio and confirm the Output Device matches your interface or headphones; check the stereo output channel strip in the Mixer is not muted
content.do_not: do not adjust track faders or EQ before confirming the output routing is correct

content.symptom: Logic's meters show activity and playback runs normally, but there is no sound from speakers or headphones; other apps may also go silent at the same time
content.cause: macOS Core Audio has entered a bad state and lost its connection to the output device — a known macOS bug
content.fix: Toggle Core Audio off and back on: Logic Pro > Settings > Audio > Devices tab > uncheck 'Enable Core Audio', wait 2 seconds, then re-enable it. If other apps are also silent, restart the Mac.
content.do_not: do not adjust faders, output routing, or plugin settings first — the issue is at the macOS audio system level

solutions.name: audio interface not recognized in Logic

content.symptom: the interface doesn't appear in Logic Pro > Settings > Audio device list, or Logic shows no input signal even with the interface connected and working in other apps
content.cause: the interface is not visible to macOS Core Audio, Logic lacks microphone privacy permission, or a driver conflict exists
content.fix: Step 1: Open macOS Audio MIDI Setup — if the interface doesn't appear there, Logic won't see it either; try a different USB port/cable. Step 2: Check System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone and ensure Logic Pro has access. Step 3: Reinstall the interface's driver if one is required.
content.do_not: do not adjust buffer size or device settings in Logic until the interface appears correctly in macOS Audio MIDI Setup

content.symptom: spinning beach ball, dropout clicks, or Logic's System Overload alert
content.cause: real-time plugin processing demand exceeds what the buffer can deliver
content.fix: increase the I/O buffer size (try 256 or 512 samples while mixing); then freeze CPU-heavy tracks (right-click the track header > Freeze Track)
content.do_not: do not dismiss the alert and keep working at the same settings — the dropout will keep happening

solutions.name: system overload on Apple Silicon Mac

content.symptom: Logic shows a 'System Overload' or 'Disk Too Slow' alert despite the Mac being a powerful M1/M2/M3/M4 machine
content.cause: Logic is not using all available CPU threads (a known issue with the 'Automatic' thread setting on Apple Silicon), or macOS Voice Isolation is adding processing overhead
content.fix: Set Processing Threads to the maximum available number rather than 'Automatic'. Change Multithreading from 'Playback and Live Tracks' to 'Playback'. Disable macOS Voice Isolation in Control Center if active. Freeze CPU-heavy tracks.
content.do_not: do not dismiss the overload alert and keep working — freeze the most CPU-intensive tracks before continuing

content.symptom: channel strip meters don't move or respond at all when you sing or play, even with a working, correctly-configured audio interface connected
content.fix: macOS System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone — toggle Logic Pro on. After granting access, quit and relaunch Logic Pro — macOS does not apply a newly granted permission to an already-running process.

content.symptom: you can hear yourself delayed by 20–50ms or more when singing or playing through Logic with software monitoring active; recorded audio appears slightly late on the timeline
content.cause: the I/O buffer size is too large, or plugins with high latency in the channel strip are adding monitoring delay (PDC)
content.fix: Step 1: Reduce the I/O buffer size to 64 or 128 samples. Step 2: Choose Record > Low Latency Monitoring Mode to bypass latency-adding plugins on record-enabled tracks. Step 3: If your interface supports direct monitoring, use that instead.
content.do_not: do not leave a large buffer and try to sing or play along to the delayed signal — the perceived delay will affect your performance and the recorded timing

content.opens: Audio settings pane, Devices tab — I/O Buffer Size pop-up menu (32 to 1024 samples). Use 64-128 samples while recording to minimize latency; switch to 256-512 while mixing to reduce CPU load.
Project Settings window, Audio tab — Sample Rate, Spatial Audio, Surround Format, Pan Law, and Apple Loops quality. Change the project's sample rate here (most commonly between 44.1 kHz and 48 kHz).
Audio settings pane, Devices tab — Processing Threads pop-up menu. Controls how many CPU threads Logic's audio engine uses; set to the maximum available rather than 'Automatic' on Apple Silicon.
Toggles Low Latency Monitoring Mode — bypasses latency-adding plugins on record-enabled tracks so software monitoring stays close to real time.
Settings window, Audio tab — output/input device selection, Core Audio on/off, sample rate, and buffer size all live here.

Opens the Configure Track Header panel, where Input Monitoring (the "I" button on audio tracks) can be checked or unchecked. If it's already checked, the button is already visible on the track header — check the current state before assuming it needs enabling.
Key Commands window — search, reassign, or add keyboard shortcuts for any Logic function. Default shortcut: Option+K.
Plug-in Manager — scan for, enable, or disable installed Audio Units plugins.

Bounce dialog — renders the entire project down to a single mixed audio file. This is how you export your final mix or master as one file (MP3, WAV, AIFF) — not separate per-track stems. Set output format, bit depth, sample rate, normalization, and bounce range. Default shortcut: Cmd+B.

File Type and Bit Depth for recorded audio, and Overlapping Track Recordings behavior. Settings window, Recording tab — Audio Recording section (File Type, e.g. WAVE/AIFF, and Bit Depth, e.g. 24-bit), MIDI Recording section (Auto Record Enable), and Overlapping Track Recordings section (Cycle Off/Cycle On/Replace behavior, set separately for MIDI and Audio — e.g. Audio Cycle On defaults to "Create Take Folder").

Turn on or enable count-in / pre-roll before recording starts, or change where recorded audio files are saved. Project Settings window, Recording tab — count-in, pre-roll, Allow tempo change recording, Automatically colorize takes, MIDI data reduction and duplicate erasure, and Audio Recording Path (the folder new recordings are saved to).
Project Settings window, Smart Tempo tab — set whether the project uses a fixed tempo, adapts to audio, or keeps the original recording tempo.
Channel EQ plugin — 8-band parametric EQ with a real-time frequency analyzer. Opened via Search and Add Plug-in (Ctrl+Cmd+P): type 'cha' to filter, then press Return.

Compressor plugin — threshold, ratio, attack, release, knee, makeup gain with multiple vintage circuit models. Opened via Search and Add Plug-in (Ctrl+Cmd+P): type 'com' to filter, then press Return. Search also matches Squash Compressor, AUMultibandCompressor, and Multipressor — Return picks whichever ranks first, which favors whatever was searched most recently, so an unrelated recent search can make this open the wrong one.

Space Designer plugin — convolution reverb for realistic room ambience and acoustic space, using a built-in impulse response library (real recorded spaces, not an algorithm) and envelope controls. Good for putting drums, vocals, or any track in a believable-sounding room. Opened via Search and Add Plug-in (Ctrl+Cmd+P): type 'spa' to filter, then press Return.

Tape Delay plugin — tempo-synced delay with tape flutter, saturation, and filter controls. Opened via Search and Add Plug-in (Ctrl+Cmd+P): type 'tape delay' to filter, then press Return. Search also matches Tru-Tape Delay — Return picks whichever ranks first, which favors whatever was searched most recently, so an unrelated recent search can make this open the wrong one.
DeEsser 2 plugin — frequency-selective dynamic compression targeting sibilant consonants. Opened via Search and Add Plug-in (Ctrl+Cmd+P): type 'dee' to filter, then press Return.
Flex Pitch enabled on the selected track. Double-click an audio region to open the Flex Pitch editor in the editor pane below the Tracks Area.

Click the Flex button on the track header (or press Cmd+F) to open the Flex dropdown — the same menu used for Flex Pitch. "Monophonic" is checked by default; below the divider choose a Flex Time algorithm: Automatic (Polyphonic), Monophonic, Slicing, Rhythmic, Polyphonic, Speed (FX), or Tempophone (FX). Use Slicing or Rhythmic for drums, Monophonic for vocals.
Automation lanes revealed on all tracks. Each lane shows the current parameter (default: Volume). Use the parameter pop-up to switch to Pan, sends, or any plugin parameter. Shortcut: A.

The Mixer — all track channel strips side by side with faders, sends, inserts, and EQ thumbnails. The All / Tracks / Single buttons at top-left control which channels are visible — switching modes accidentally is a common cause of channels appearing to disappear. Shortcut: X (toggle in main window), Cmd+2 (floating window).
Smart Controls panel at the bottom of the main window — simplified controls for the selected track's instruments and effects. Automatically changes based on which track is selected. Shortcut: B.
Loop Browser panel — search Apple Loops by instrument, genre, mood, or keyword. Green loops are Apple Loops that stretch to match project tempo; purple loops are fixed-tempo audio files. Shortcut: O.

Bounce in Place — render a region with its effects baked in: commits/prints the selected region's track plugins permanently into new audio, in place, so they're no longer separately editable afterward. Opens the Bounce in Place dialog. Select a region first, then press Ctrl+B. Also accessible by right-clicking a region and choosing Bounce or Join > Bounce In Place.

Export dialog — exports each track as a separate individual audio file (stems), one file per track — this is NOT a single mixed-down file (for a single final mixed file, use Bounce Project, Cmd+B, instead). Options for format, bit depth, sample rate, and whether to include the master effects chain. Shortcut: Shift+Cmd+E. Menu path: File > Export > All Tracks as Audio Files...

Freeze renders the track's plugins to a temporary audio file and disables them, freeing CPU. Press Option+T to open Configure Track Header, then check Freeze under Buttons (this also puts a snowflake icon on the track header). Click the snowflake on the track header to freeze; click again to unfreeze.

Piano Roll editor — MIDI note data as horizontal bars on a grid. Fastest access: double-click any MIDI region. The lower-right corner of a note resizes its length; drag from the body to move it. Shortcut: Cmd+4.

Drummer Editor panel (header reads 'Session Player') — appears only when a Drummer region is selected. Three tabs: Main (separate Complexity and Intensity sliders — not a combined XY pad — plus per-instrument kit-piece density selectors, Fill Amount/Fill Complexity/Swing knobs, and a Follow Rhythm Of control (in the kick/snare row's pattern popover) that follows either the Chords track or a specific track), Details (Ghost Notes, Feel, Dynamics, and Humanize knobs, plus Snare/Percussion/Hi-Hat type and Tempo dropdowns), and Manual (click-to-program step grid for hand-placed hits). Change genre and drummer character in the Library panel (shortcut: Y).

Retroactively captures MIDI played during the last playback pass — even without being in record mode — and creates a new MIDI region. Works for MIDI only, not audio. The buffer clears when you stop and play again without capturing. Shortcut: Shift+R. Also accessible via the Flashback Capture button in the control bar.

Project Settings window, MIDI tab — Chase section controls whether Logic re-triggers notes, controllers, and program changes when playback starts mid-section. If held chords don't sound when starting playback in the middle of a section, enable Chase > Notes here.

Global Tracks area above the Tracks Area — Tempo, Time Signature, Key, Marker, Movie, Transposition, and Beat Mapping tracks that apply to the whole project. Right-click the header to choose which tracks are visible. The Tempo track is where you automate tempo changes. Shortcut: G.

Cycle mode — Logic loops playback between the yellow markers in the ruler. Recording while cycle is active creates Take Folders by default (one take per pass) — this default is configurable in Recording Settings. Drag in the ruler area to set the cycle region. Shortcut: C.

Adaptive Limiter — look-ahead brickwall limiter with Output Ceiling and Gain controls. Set Out Ceiling to -0.1 dB (not 0 dB) to prevent inter-sample clipping on streaming platforms. Typically the last insert on the Stereo Out. Opened via Search and Add Plug-in (Ctrl+Cmd+P): type 'ada' to filter, then press Return.

Multipressor — Logic's multiband compressor. Splits the signal into up to 4 frequency bands with independent compression per band. Useful on a master or drum bus to control dynamics in specific frequency ranges without affecting overall tonal balance. Opened via Search and Add Plug-in (Ctrl+Cmd+P): type 'multip' to filter, then press Return.

Stereo Spread — widens the stereo image by separating frequencies across the left-right field. Upper frequencies spread wider; lower frequencies stay centered. Keep bass mono — the lower frequency bands intentionally have reduced spread. Opened via Search and Add Plug-in (Ctrl+Cmd+P): type 'stereo sp' to filter, then press Return.

Project Settings window, Smart Tempo tab, 'Defaults for Flex and Smart Tempo Region Setting' section — 'Set Imported Files To' dropdown. Controls whether Flex is applied by default to newly imported audio files. Set to 'Flex Off' to prevent Logic from automatically stretching/warping imported samples and loops to match project tempo. This is a per-project setting, not a global preference.

Project Settings window, Metronome tab — controls click sound, volume, and whether the click plays during recording only or also during playback. To hear the click only during recording, right-click the metronome button in the control bar and choose Click While Recording.

Press K to toggle the click on and off — a global key command, works no matter what's selected or in focus. To hear the click only while recording (not during playback), right-click the metronome button in the control bar (just left of the tempo/LCD display) and choose Click While Recording. For click sound, volume, or other detailed options, see Metronome Settings.

Event List editor — all MIDI events as a numerical list with exact position, pitch, velocity, and length. Useful for removing unwanted pitch bend data or stray controller messages sent by a hardware keyboard. Shortcut: Cmd+7.

Quantize pop-up in the Region Inspector — snaps MIDI notes to the nearest rhythmic grid division. Non-destructive: changing the value updates the region live. For swing/shuffle feel, adjust the Q-Swing slider below the Quantize pop-up. Shortcut: Q (applies current value), I (open Inspector).
Disables all control surface communication, including MIDI controllers Logic has detected as control surfaces. If your MIDI keyboard works in other apps but not in Logic, try this first.

solutions.name: follow tempo
aliases: stop region from stretching to tempo

content.opens: Region Inspector (select an audio region, press I) — click the 'Region:' disclosure header to expand it if collapsed, revealing a 'Smart Tempo' dropdown (there is no 'Follow Tempo' checkbox, despite common phrasing/older docs). Options: Off, On, On + Align Bars, On + Align Bars and Beats. Set to Off to stop this specific region from stretching to match project tempo, overriding the project-wide Smart Tempo setting for that region only. The expanded Region box also shows Mute, Loop, Quantize, Q-Swing, Transpose, Fine Tune, Pitch Source, Flex, File Tempo, and Gain. It edits whichever region(s) are selected; with nothing selected the Region box reads 'Audio Defaults' and the change applies to new regions instead. Before the user runs it, ask them to select the region to change, or clear the selection to change the default.

Remove Silence dialog — automatically splits a region at quiet sections below a threshold, creating multiple shorter regions from one long one. Adjust Threshold, Minimum Time to Accept as Silence, and Pre/Post Attack/Release to avoid clipping phrase starts and ends. Key Command name: 'Remove Silence from Audio Region'. Shortcut: Ctrl+X on a selected audio region.

Mastering Assistant — AI-driven mastering that analyzes the mix and applies EQ, compression, and limiting to match a target loudness. Requires Apple Silicon (M1 or later) and Logic Pro 10.7.5 or later.

ChromaVerb plugin — Logic's algorithmic reverb with 14 room types, a visual frequency-response display, and per-frequency-band damping controls. Better for creative and musical reverb; Space Designer is better for realistic acoustic spaces using impulse responses. Opened via Search and Add Plug-in (Ctrl+Cmd+P): type 'chromav' to filter (not 'chroma' — collides with ChromaGlow), then press Return.

Creates a new Audio track directly, with a channel strip ready for recording or importing audio — this is the track type for recording vocals or any live instrument. Faster than the general New Tracks… dialog when you already know you want an audio track. Shortcut: Option+Cmd+A (also Track > New Audio Track).

Creates a new Software Instrument track directly, ready to load an instrument plugin. Faster than the general New Tracks… dialog when you already know you want a software instrument. Shortcut: Option+Cmd+S (also Track > New Software Instrument Track).

Creates a new External MIDI track — routes MIDI to an external hardware synth or sound module rather than a software instrument inside Logic. Shortcut: Option+Cmd+X (also Track > New External MIDI Track).

Opens the New Session Player Track dialog — Logic's session players (Drummer and other AI performers) generate parts that follow the song. Shortcut: Option+Cmd+U (also Track > New Session Player SI Track…). See the drummer editor entry for editing an existing Drummer region.

solutions.name: new track with duplicate settings
aliases: copy channel strip to new track

content.opens: Creates a new track with the same channel strip settings (inserts, sends, routing) as the currently selected track, but no audio/MIDI content copied. Use New Track With Duplicate Settings and Content (Track > Other) instead to also duplicate the region content. Shortcut: Cmd+D.

New Tracks dialog — choose the track type (Audio, Software Instrument, External MIDI, or a Session Player) and how many to create, in one place, before anything is created. Use this when you're not yet sure which specific type you want; if you already know, the direct shortcuts are faster (Option+Cmd+A audio, Option+Cmd+S software instrument, Option+Cmd+X external MIDI, Option+Cmd+U session player). Menu: Track > New Tracks… (shortcut Option+Cmd+N).

content.zone: low-mid buildup, roughly 150–350 Hz; acoustic boom at 80–120 Hz
content.add_when: intentionally warm, lo-fi, or vintage guitar tone
content.add_move: gentle low-shelf boost below 250 Hz; ease or remove the high-pass filter
content.remove_when: guitars sound thick, boomy, or are cluttering the low end and making the mix congested
content.remove_move: high-pass filter at 80–120 Hz on electric guitar (100–150 Hz on acoustic) to remove low-end bleed; narrow bell cut at 200–350 Hz to reduce body buildup
content.do_not: do not skip the high-pass filter on guitars — the low end they add below 80 Hz almost never helps the mix and always fights the kick and bass

content.zone: low-mid buildup across multiple tracks, 150–400 Hz
content.add_when: intentional lo-fi, dense, or warm full-mix texture
content.add_move: remove high-pass filters from elements you want to be warm; add subtle low-shelf boost on a group bus
content.remove_when: the mix sounds congested, elements are hard to distinguish, or the low-mid is overwhelming
content.remove_move: high-pass filter every element that doesn't need low end — vocals, guitars, synths, keys; set the cutoff just above each element's lowest meaningful frequency
content.do_not: do not reach for the master bus EQ first; fix mud at the individual track level

content.zone: presence zone, roughly 2–5 kHz
content.add_when: intentionally aggressive, cutting, or gritty vocal tone
content.add_move: bell boost +2–3 dB somewhere in 2–5 kHz; narrow Q to stay surgical
content.remove_when: vocals are fatiguing, sharp, or feel like they're cutting too hard
content.remove_move: narrow bell cut 2–4 dB somewhere in the 2–5 kHz range — sweep slowly because the exact frequency that sounds harsh varies by voice
content.do_not: do not add a broad high-shelf cut — you'll dull the whole vocal trying to fix one frequency

content.zone: upper presence/air, 6–14 kHz; metallic clang at 3–5 kHz
content.add_when: intentionally bright, cutting, or aggressive hi-hat sound
content.add_move: high-shelf boost above 10 kHz; or bell boost at 3–5 kHz for metallic edge
content.remove_when: hi-hats are fatiguing, sizzly, or feel like they're slicing through the mix uncomfortably
content.remove_move: gentle high-shelf cut above 10–12 kHz; or narrow bell cut at 3–5 kHz for metallic clang specifically
content.do_not: do not low-pass aggressively — you'll remove all the air and the hat will sound dull and closed

content.zone: high shelf, 10–14 kHz
content.add_when: vocals feel closed, dull, or lack shimmer and openness
content.add_move: try a gentle high-shelf boost starting around +2 dB at 10–12 kHz — listen carefully after each small adjustment
content.remove_when: vocals sound glassy, harsh in the very top end, or are causing listening fatigue
content.remove_move: gentle high-shelf cut above 10–12 kHz, or reduce any existing high-shelf boost
content.do_not: do not go above +4 dB on the shelf without de-essing first — adding air can expose sibilance

content.zone: low-mid body, 150–300 Hz
content.add_when: vocals sound thin, brittle, or lacking body
content.add_move: gentle low-shelf or bell boost starting at +1–2 dB around 200–250 Hz
content.remove_when: vocals sound boxy, congested, or are fighting the bass and kick
content.remove_move: narrow bell cut 1–3 dB in the 200–350 Hz range
content.do_not: do not boost past +3 dB in this zone without also listening for mud — warmth and mud share the same frequencies

content.zone: low-mid body, 150–300 Hz; dynamic control
content.add_when: intentionally transparent, clean, or airy vocal sound with no low-mid weight
content.add_move: high-pass filter to remove low-mid weight; ease any compression
content.remove_when: vocals lack body, feel weak, or disappear in a dense mix
content.remove_move: gentle bell or low-shelf boost at 150–250 Hz; add gentle compression to bring up the sustained body
content.do_not: do not keep stacking more EQ boosts — if one approach isn't working, try compression instead

content.zone: transient energy — kick and snare attack, 60–200 Hz (weight) and 2–5 kHz (click/crack)
content.add_when: the mix needs more impact, drive, and physical energy
content.add_move: slow down compressor attack times on drums to let transients through before compression engages (try 20–40ms); add subtle saturation on the drum bus; boost kick beater click at 3–5 kHz
content.remove_when: intentionally smooth, soft, or lo-fi production where transients should be gentle
content.remove_move: faster compressor attack to clamp transients; gentle limiting on individual elements
content.do_not: do not increase the master bus limiter gain to try to add punch — that compresses transients further and makes the problem worse

content.zone: sub weight at 60–80 Hz; beater click at 3–5 kHz; boxiness at 200–400 Hz
content.add_when: kick needs more impact, weight, or presence
content.add_move: boost 60–80 Hz for sub weight; boost 3–5 kHz for beater click; cut 200–400 Hz if the kick sounds boxy
content.remove_when: intentionally soft, pillowy, or low-impact kick
content.remove_move: reduce sub boost; apply a faster compressor attack to soften the transient
content.do_not: do not boost sub and click without also cutting the boxy 200–400 Hz zone — that range muddies the low end

content.zone: body at 150–250 Hz; crack at 1–3 kHz
content.add_when: intentionally tight, clicky, or high-pitched snare with no low weight
content.add_move: high-pass the snare to remove low-mid body; cut the 200 Hz zone
content.remove_when: snare sounds weak, papery, or has no thump
content.remove_move: bell boost at 150–200 Hz for body; add compression with a medium attack (30–50 ms) to bring up the sustain
content.do_not: do not reach for a sample layer as the first move — try EQ and compression on the recorded sound first

content.zone: low-mid boxiness, roughly 250–450 Hz
content.add_when: intentional lo-fi, vintage telephone, or transistor-radio effect
content.add_move: bell boost at 300–400 Hz; band-pass filter to remove frequencies above and below
content.remove_when: the mix sounds like it's inside a cardboard box — congested, honky, or unclear in the midrange
content.remove_move: solo each track to find the main offender; narrow bell cut 2–4 dB at the culprit frequency in the 250–450 Hz range; high-pass all non-bass tracks above their lowest useful frequency
content.do_not: do not apply a master bus EQ cut to fix boxiness that exists across multiple individual tracks — fix it at the source tracks

content.zone: reverb wash across the full frequency spectrum
content.add_when: intentionally atmospheric, dreamy, or ambient — shoegaze, ambient, certain pop productions
content.add_move: increase send levels to reverb Aux buses; use longer decay times (2–4 seconds); reduce pre-delay so reverb starts immediately after the source
content.remove_when: the mix sounds distant, unfocused, or all elements blur together in reverb
content.remove_move: reduce send levels to the reverb Aux first; add a high-pass filter on the reverb Aux to remove muddy low-mid reverb; increase pre-delay to 20–40ms to create space between the dry signal and reverb tail; try a shorter room preset instead of a hall
content.do_not: do not add more compression to try to bring elements forward out of the wash — reduce the reverb level instead

content.zone: presence and clarity zone, 1–5 kHz; also level relative to drums and instruments
content.add_when: intentionally recessed, background, or atmospheric vocal treatment
content.add_move: reduce vocal fader; add more reverb send; cut presence at 2–4 kHz
content.remove_when: the vocal exists in the mix but is hard to hear, masked by instruments, or disappears during the chorus
content.remove_move: cut the competing instruments in the 1–5 kHz presence zone where the vocal lives; add a gentle bell boost at 2–4 kHz on the vocal; verify reverb is on a send (not a 50% wet insert which pushes vocals back); check the vocal fader level relative to the drum overhead level
content.do_not: do not just raise the vocal fader without also carving space in the competing instruments — a louder vocal without frequency carving still sounds buried

content.zone: upper low-mid, roughly 500–1000 Hz
content.add_when: intentional nasal or telephone-filter character (certain retro or stylized effects)
content.add_move: bell boost at 500–800 Hz; narrow Q; pair with a low-pass filter to enhance the telephone effect
content.remove_when: vocals sound honky, nasal, or like they're coming through a cardboard tube
content.remove_move: narrow bell cut 2–4 dB somewhere in the 500–1000 Hz range — sweep slowly to find the exact frequency that sounds most honky on this specific voice while it plays
content.do_not: do not boost high frequencies to try to mask the nasal quality — remove the problem frequency first, then assess

content.symptom: red clip indicators on the channel; audible crackle or distortion
content.cause: signal level peaks above 0 dBFS
content.fix: reduce the track's clip gain (right-click the region) or the channel fader until peaks stay below 0 dBFS; then add a Compressor (fast attack around 5ms, ratio around 8:1) to catch fast peaks before they clip again
content.do_not: do not apply EQ or effects to a clipping signal — fix the gain first, then shape the sound

content.symptom: sharp, hissing 's' and 'sh' sounds that stick out above the rest of the vocal
content.cause: peaks of energy in the 6–10 kHz range on fricative consonants
content.fix: insert a DeEsser plugin and set the detection frequency to 6–10 kHz; reduce the amount until the 's' sounds are tamed but not completely removed
content.do_not: do not apply a static high-shelf cut to fix sibilance — it dulls the entire vocal, not just the problem moments

content.symptom: low-frequency thump or pop on 'p' and 'b' sounds
content.cause: air burst from the singer's mouth hitting the microphone capsule directly
content.fix: apply a steep high-pass filter (around 18 dB/oct) at 80–120 Hz on the vocal channel; for very severe plosives, automate the volume down on the specific syllable instead
content.do_not: do not boost the high end to try to mask the thump — the pop is a low-frequency problem and must be removed, not covered

content.symptom: a sustained, pitched ringing sound after the snare hit — often metallic or tonal
content.cause: a narrow resonance peak at a specific frequency, usually in the 200–800 Hz range
content.fix: use a narrow bell notch cut (high Q) and slowly sweep between 200 and 800 Hz while the track plays until the ring is reduced; cut 4–8 dB at that frequency
content.do_not: do not gate the snare to cut the ring — gating changes the feel and timing of the snare; a notch cut removes the ring while keeping the natural decay

solutions.name: AU plugin not showing up in Logic

content.symptom: a third-party plugin doesn't appear in Logic's plugin picker, or shows as 'Crashed' or 'Failed' in the Plugin Manager even after reinstalling
content.cause: corrupted Audio Unit cache — Logic's cached validation results are stale or corrupt after a macOS update, Logic update, or plugin update
content.fix: Step 1: Quit Logic. Step 2: Delete the AU cache file at ~/Library/Caches/com.apple.audiounits.cache — Logic rebuilds it on next launch and rescans all plugins fresh. Step 3: Relaunch Logic and open the Plugin Manager to check the status. If still failing, reinstall the plugin from the developer's full installer.
content.do_not: do not keep clicking 'Recover' in the crash dialog — it loops back to the same result; deleting the cache is the actual fix

solutions.name: MIDI keyboard not triggering notes in Logic

content.symptom: playing the keyboard produces no notes in Logic; the keyboard works in other apps or in macOS Audio MIDI Setup but not in Logic; or the keyboard worked before and suddenly stopped
content.cause: Logic has registered the controller as a control surface instead of a MIDI instrument, a macOS driver issue, or a USB power problem
content.fix: Step 1: Try Logic Pro > Control Surfaces > Bypass All Control Surfaces — some keyboards are detected as control surfaces which prevents them from sending MIDI notes to tracks. Step 2: Confirm the keyboard appears in macOS Audio MIDI Setup. Step 3: Plug the keyboard directly into the Mac rather than through a USB hub. Step 4: Create a new empty project and test — the issue may be project-specific routing.
content.do_not: do not spend time adjusting Logic's MIDI settings before confirming the keyboard appears in macOS Audio MIDI Setup

solutions.name: iCloud corrupting or losing Logic project files

content.symptom: a Logic project stored on iCloud opens empty, shows 'Audio Files Not Found' errors for all regions, or audio regions appear grayed out; the project worked locally but broke when opened on another Mac or after iCloud synced
content.cause: iCloud's file-on-demand system converts files inside the Logic project bundle to '.icloud' placeholder stubs to save local space — Logic cannot read these placeholders and treats them as missing audio
content.fix: Move the project off iCloud to a local folder. To recover: in Finder, navigate inside the project bundle (right-click > Show Package Contents), find any .icloud placeholder files, right-click each and choose 'Download Now'. After all files download, move the whole project to a local drive before opening.
content.do_not: do not store active Logic project bundles directly inside iCloud Drive — the .logicx bundle contains many small files that iCloud aggressively offloads to the cloud

content.symptom: Logic quits immediately after the splash screen before loading a project; the crash report mentions CoreML, EXC_CRASH, SIGABRT, or references com.apple.coreml
content.cause: corrupted Logic Pro application cache, typically triggered by a failed or interrupted update; the CoreML crash specifically affects Logic 11.1.x
content.fix: Delete Logic Pro from the Applications folder, then reinstall it from the App Store. Your projects, settings, and sound library are completely unaffected — only the application binary is removed. If the crash persists, also delete ~/Library/Caches/com.apple.logic.pro and relaunch.
content.do_not: do not attempt to repair the application by replacing individual files — a clean reinstall from the App Store is faster and more reliable than any partial fix

solutions.name: Logic AI features grayed out on Apple Silicon

content.symptom: Mastering Assistant, Stem Splitter, or other AI-powered features appear grayed out or unavailable on an M1/M2/M3/M4 Mac
content.cause: Logic Pro is running under Rosetta 2 Intel emulation mode instead of natively on Apple Silicon — these features require the native ARM build and Apple's Neural Engine
content.fix: In Finder, navigate to Applications, right-click Logic Pro > Get Info. If 'Open using Rosetta' is checked, uncheck it, close Get Info, and relaunch Logic. The AI features will be available after relaunching natively.
content.do_not: do not reinstall Logic expecting this to fix itself — the Rosetta checkbox persists across reinstalls if not explicitly unchecked in Get Info

solutions.name: Sound Library missing or not downloading after Logic update

content.symptom: patches, loops, or instrument sounds are missing after a Logic update; downloads fail with 'Check your Internet connection' even on a fast connection; or downloads appear to complete but content is still absent
content.cause: the Logic update requires a new version of the Sound Library, or the Sound Library was relocated to an external drive that Logic can no longer find
content.fix: Step 1: Logic Pro > Sound Library > Download All Available Sounds. Step 2: If downloads fail, update Logic Pro to the latest version first (App Store > Updates), then retry — some library versions only work with specific Logic versions. Step 3: If the library was moved to an external drive, reconnect the drive and confirm its name hasn't changed since Logic configured the path.
content.do_not: do not delete and reinstall Logic to fix missing sounds — the application and the Sound Library are stored separately; reinstalling Logic does not restore downloaded content

solutions.name: MIDI notes silent when starting playback mid-section

content.symptom: when you start playback from the middle of a section, held chords or sustained notes that should already be playing are silent until a new Note On event arrives in the timeline
content.cause: MIDI Chase is disabled — Logic is not re-triggering Note On messages whose start position is earlier than the current playhead
content.fix: Enable MIDI Chase: File > Project Settings > MIDI > Chase tab > check 'Notes'. You can also enable chase for Program Changes, Pitch Bend, and Controllers in the same panel for complete chase behavior.
content.do_not: do not move the MIDI notes forward in the Piano Roll as a workaround — enable Chase instead; moving notes changes the musical timing

solutions.name: clicks and pops at take folder edit points

content.symptom: after comping takes in a Take Folder, there are audible clicks or pops at the boundaries where the comp switches from one take to another
content.cause: the edit points between takes have no crossfade — the audio waveform is cut abruptly, creating a discontinuity in the waveform
content.fix: Select the Crossfade tool (press X with the pointer tool active in the Tracks Area) and drag across the edit point to create a 5–10ms crossfade. Alternatively, after comping, select the Take Folder, use Edit > Select All to select all comp regions, then apply crossfades via the Crossfade tool across all boundaries at once.
content.do_not: do not re-record takes to eliminate clicks — crossfades at edit points are the standard fix for this in any DAW

solutions.name: unwanted pitch bend data on MIDI recordings

content.symptom: recorded MIDI notes sound slightly sharp or flat, or pitch bends unexpectedly during playback; the Event List shows pitch bend (PBND) events you did not intentionally play
content.cause: the pitch bend wheel or joystick on the MIDI controller was slightly off-center when recording started, sending a continuous pitch bend offset throughout the recording
content.fix: Open the Piano Roll for the affected region, switch to the Event List (Cmd+7), filter to show Pitch Bend events (click the filter button and select Controller/Pitch Bend), select all pitch bend events, and delete them. Before your next recording, ensure the pitch wheel returns fully to center — some controllers have a spring mechanism that can stick slightly off-center.
content.do_not: do not try to fix pitch bend artifacts with Flex Pitch — the root cause is MIDI controller data that must be removed from the MIDI region itself

content.fix: Add a Compressor to the bass (or target) track. In the plugin's top-right corner, find the Sidechain Input dropdown (easy to miss) and set it to the kick track or bus — this is the step most people can't find. Lower the threshold until the kick reliably triggers ducking. Ratio 4:1 to 8:1 for a subtle duck (20:1+ for an exaggerated EDM pump). Fast attack (1-3ms) for a tight duck on every hit; release around 80-150ms, matched loosely to the kick's decay.
content.do_not: third-party plugins may not expose a sidechain input — use Logic's stock Compressor if yours doesn't have one

content.fix: Send the track (or drum bus) to an Aux via a Send, add a Compressor to the Aux with aggressive settings (high ratio, low threshold), then blend the Aux return in under the dry signal — subtle blending usually sounds most natural. The dry signal preserves the transient snap while the compressed copy adds sustain and density.
content.do_not: do not replace the dry signal — parallel compression only works because the uncompressed original is still present alongside the compressed copy

content.fix: Add a saturation plugin (Phat FX's Distortion module for subtle-to-moderate character, Bitcrusher for heavier digital grit) and start with the drive very low — bring it up until the tone changes slightly. Saturation adds harmonic overtones that make a thin or digital-sounding vocal feel richer and more present without necessarily raising its measured level.
content.do_not: do not push the drive until the effect is obviously audible — it usually works best when you can't quite tell it's there

content.fix: Set each track to peak around -12 dBFS before any plugins (adjust with clip gain — right-click the region — rather than the fader, which should stay near 0 dB). Leave 3-6 dB of headroom on the master bus, aiming for peaks around -6 dBFS on the Stereo Out before the limiter. Set the Adaptive Limiter's Out Ceiling to -0.1 dB, not 0 dB, to avoid inter-sample clipping on streaming platforms.
content.do_not: do not rely on the mixer alone to protect you — Logic's mixer is 32-bit float and won't clip internally, but third-party plugins and your interface's analog outputs will

content.fix: Click the disclosure triangle on the Take Folder region to expand it and see individual takes stacked below. Use Quick Swipe Comping — drag across the portion of a take you want; drag a different take's lane to switch takes for that section. Once satisfied, use Flatten and Merge to create one continuous audio file (Flatten alone keeps separate regions); both preserve the original takes inside the folder until explicitly deleted.
content.do_not: do not add heavy processing before flattening — apply plugins to the single clean flattened file, not across the raw take boundaries

content.fix: Freeze CPU-heavy tracks — especially virtual instruments with large sample sets and tracks with convolution reverb or linear-phase EQ. A frozen track renders to a temporary file and disables its plugins, using almost no CPU while sounding identical. Freeze early and often when building a dense session; just remember to unfreeze a track before editing it.

Have the singer perform the same part again on a new take (a real double always sounds more authentic than a simulated one). Pan the main vocal center and the double to one side (or spread doubles hard left/right for backing vocals); set the double 3-6 dB quieter than the main vocal so it thickens without competing. If a real double isn't available, a Chorus plugin or a slight pitch shift (±7-15 cents) can approximate it, though less naturally.
content.do_not: do not rely on a pitch-shifted simulated double as your first choice — the pitch/timing variation of a real second take always sounds better and avoids comb filtering

content.fix: Build a mastering chain on the Stereo Out (or a dedicated Mastering Aux): Linear Phase EQ first to correct tonal balance, then a Compressor (low ratio 1.5:1-2:1, slow attack 30-60ms, auto release, 1-3 dB gain reduction) for glue, then the Adaptive Limiter last. Set the Limiter's Out Ceiling to -0.1 dB (not 0 dB) to avoid inter-sample clipping after streaming platforms re-encode, and raise Gain until loudness is competitive without audibly squashing transients — most platforms target around -14 LUFS integrated.
content.do_not: do not set the limiter's Out Ceiling to 0 dB — it causes inter-sample peaks that distort after streaming platform encoding

content.fix: Standard order: 1) High-Pass Filter around 80-100 Hz to remove rumble and proximity effect. 2) Noise Gate (optional) if there's background noise between phrases. 3) EQ to fix tonal problems — cut mud at 200-400 Hz, cut harshness at 2-5 kHz — before compression reacts to them. 4) Compressor, 3:1 to 5:1 ratio, medium attack (10-20ms) to let consonants through. 5) De-Esser (6-10 kHz) after compression, since compression can bring sibilance up. 6) Reverb and delay on Aux sends only, never as inserts at 50% wet — keep the send return at 100% wet.
content.do_not: do not de-ess before compression — compression brings up quiet moments and can make sibilance worse after the de-esser already ran

content.fix: Open Flex Pitch on the vocal region, then work note-by-note using its six hotspots per block: drag the top-center to move a note to a new pitch, top-left/right to fix pitch drift at the start/end of a note, bottom-left for vibrato depth, bottom-right for fine pitch and formant. When shifting a note more than 2-3 semitones, drag the formant hotspot to avoid a chipmunk effect. To snap everything to the nearest semitone (a heavy auto-tune effect), select all notes (Cmd+A) and drag any note's Fine Pitch hotspot to 0.
content.do_not: do not change the Flex algorithm after editing — it destroys all edits already made on that track; if Logic splits one word into many tiny fragments, bounce the region in place first (Ctrl+B) so the algorithm has a clean file to analyze

content.fix: Enable Flex Time on the track, then choose the right algorithm for the material: Rhythmic for most drums and percussive material (adds crossfades at edit points, the best all-around choice); Slicing also works for drums with distinct hits but can click without crossfades; Monophonic for a single-note instrument like bass or solo vocal; Polyphonic only for chord-playing instruments like guitar or piano — never use it on drums, it smears cymbals.
content.do_not: do not change the algorithm after placing flex markers — it deletes all the markers and you'll have to redo the edits

problems.name: song sounds slowed
problems.note: seed_weight is a population prior, not a ranking to execute — override it whenever on-screen or AX evidence points elsewhere.

solutions.distinguisher: if speed and pitch are both off together, it's the sample rate, not the tempo — tempo changes preserve pitch, a true sample-rate mismatch does not
affects one imported region specifically, and pitch stays correct (it's time-stretching) — not a project-wide speed+pitch shift

problems.name: mix sounds muddy
problems.note: ask which element (bass, vocals, guitars, or kick-vs-bass specifically) if the query doesn't say — if no element stands out, it may be a general multi-track issue.

solutions.distinguisher: the low end specifically (bass) sounds unclear or soupy — not the vocals, not the overall mix
vocals specifically sound masked or hard to hear — not the low end
kick and bass sound like one indistinct blob or cancel each other, not just general low-mid buildup
specifically the guitars sound thick, boomy, or are cluttering the low end — not the bass or vocals
the mud isn't isolated to one element — general congestion across many tracks with no clear single culprit
wants the specific sidechain-compression technique/settings for kick-vs-bass, not just a diagnosis of the clash

problems.name: song sounds thin or hollow
aliases: my song sounds thin and hollow on my phone speaker
mix loses body on small speakers
problems.note: genuinely three-way ambiguous without more information — ask which listening context and whether it's the low end or the stereo width that feels missing.

solutions.distinguisher: thinness is about missing sub weight — check if it's specifically the low end that feels absent
thinness is about excessive stereo widening causing a hollow center
thinness only shows up on mono/small-speaker playback specifically but sounds fine and full in stereo — a phase-cancellation signature

problems.name: no sound / silent output
problems.note: if other apps are also silent at the same time, that points to Core Audio specifically, not an in-app routing issue.

solutions.distinguisher: only Logic is silent — other apps make sound fine, and it's a routing/mute issue inside Logic itself
other apps go silent at the same time, or it happened suddenly mid-session with no setting changed — a macOS-level issue, not a Logic setting

solutions.distinguisher: causes a full pitch+speed shift, not just crackle/pops — a red flag if speed or pitch also sound wrong, not just glitchy
gets worse as you add more tracks/plugins, or Logic shows a System Overload message — a load problem, not a rate problem

wants to reduce CPU load by freezing specific heavy tracks, as an addition to lowering overall load

problems.name: vocals or hi-hats sound harsh
problems.note: ask which element if the query doesn't say — vocals and hi-hats harshness live in very different frequency zones (2-5 kHz vs 6-14 kHz).

solutions.distinguisher: specifically the vocals sound fatiguing or sharp — presence-zone (2-5 kHz) issue
specifically the hi-hats/cymbals sound sizzly or metallic — a much higher zone (6-14 kHz) or metallic clang at 3-5 kHz

problems.name: vocal tone needs adjusting
aliases: how do i improve vocal tone
problems.note: three distinct directions — ask whether they want more air/brightness, more warmth/body, or are specifically complaining the vocals sound thin/weak.

solutions.distinguisher: wants more shimmer, openness, or brightness — high-shelf territory (10-14 kHz)
wants more warmth, fullness, or body — low-mid boost territory (150-300 Hz)
vocals actively sound weak or thin or disappear in the mix — needs low-mid boost plus compression, not just an EQ boost
wants a saturation/harmonic-distortion approach to warmth rather than an EQ boost

problems.name: mix lacks punch
problems.note: ask if it's kick-specific or the whole mix/drum bus in general.

solutions.distinguisher: the whole mix or drum bus lacks impact — not specifically the kick
specifically the kick lacks impact, weight, or click — not the whole mix
wants the parallel-compression technique specifically — blending a heavily compressed copy with the dry signal for density without losing transient snap

problems.name: snare sounds thin
problems.note: only one common cause for this exact symptom — no need to ask which, just confirm it's the snare and not another element.
